purpose: Recheck all five jurisdiction observation references against official primary sources. This proposal neither changes research/reviews.json nor accepts claims, activates gameplay, or establishes legal or certification approval.

preserves.note: Older evidence remains unchanged; this dated check supplements it.

references.historicalClaim: Cloud consumers assess their systems and shared responsibilities; assessment evidence informs an authorising officer and is not unconditional approval of every customer configuration.
references.historicalSourceDate: Original page published 2020-07-27; last reviewed 2024-01-18. Claim first checked 2026-11-03.
references.currentFinding: The source page remains available and calls for assessment against consumer requirements/risk tolerance, documented shared responsibilities, review of reports before authorisation, and ongoing monitoring. The current IRAP Consumer Guide page was last reviewed 2026-06-17; it requires defined assessment scope/deliverables and says the report informs a risk-based system decision. The official IRAP resources page lists 2026 program materials.

checkedSources.title: Cloud assessment and authorisation
checkedSources.supports: Consumer assessment, shared responsibility, assessment reports and ongoing monitoring.

checkedSources.title: IRAP consumer guide
checkedSources.supports: Defined assessment scope and risk-based decision for a system.

checkedSources.title: IRAP resources
checkedSources.supports: Current program material is newer than the original linked page.

references.jurisdictionAndScope: Australia; Australian government cloud-assessment and IRAP consumer guidance, not universal accreditation.
uncertainty: Specific PSPF/ISM controls, classification, entity policy, service scope, residual risk and authorising decision remain deployment-specific.
No legal eligibility or platform-wide approval is inferred.
references.proposedClaim: For an Australian government system, use assessment evidence for its stated service and scope, document shared responsibilities and consumer controls, and make and monitor a separate risk-based authorisation decision for the deployed system. IRAP evidence is not blanket approval of every configuration or customer system.
references.linkedRequirement: Represent assessment scope, consumer controls, residual risks, conditional authorisation and ongoing changes separately; do not treat IRAP assessment as blanket platform approval.

references.historicalClaim: FedRAMP evidence can be reused while an agency authorises its own system, configuration and integrations, with agency responsibilities and mission risk.
references.currentFinding: The agency-use page says certification is reusable evidence but each agency authorizes its own federal information system and accepts risk for its information, configuration, integrations, and agency-operated controls. The separate scope page says only an agency can decide whether its use is in scope. On 2026-11-04 optional early adoption has begun; mandatory adoption is scheduled for 2027-01-01, subject to area-specific applicability/effective dates.

checkedSources.title: Using a FedRAMP Certified Cloud Service
checkedSources.supports: Reusable evidence and agency system authorization, configuration, integration and ongoing responsibilities.

checkedSources.title: Scope of FedRAMP
checkedSources.supports: Use-case specific agency scope determination; not every internet service is in scope.

checkedSources.title: Important Dates for the Consolidated Rules for 2026
checkedSources.supports: Optional adoption from 2026-07-04; mandatory date 2027-01-01, with area-specific qualifications.

references.jurisdictionAndScope: US federal systems/use cases within FedRAMP scope. Does not establish DoD, classified, national-security-system or other defense eligibility.
uncertainty: Agency determines scope and applicable certification class/version for the actual use.
The 2027-01-01 mandatory transition is future-dated at this check; individual rule areas have separate applicability.
Do not apply FedRAMP to every agency internet service or infer defense approval.
references.proposedClaim: For a federal use within FedRAMP scope, reuse applicable offering evidence but authorize the agency system and assess its information, certified offering version, configuration, integrations and agency-operated controls. The agency decides scope. Apply the rules effective for the decision date; do not infer defense eligibility.
references.linkedRequirement: Separate a fictional cloud offering’s assessment/certification from an agency system authorisation; preserve version-specific terminology and do not infer defence eligibility from civilian evidence.

references.historicalClaim: ISMAP evaluates and registers services for government procurement, distinguishes the main program and low-impact SaaS, and describes procurement from lists as the principle.
references.currentFinding: The official Japanese overview remains available, describes service-level review/list registration, ISMAP-LIU for SaaS processing lower-risk business/information, and procurement from applicable lists in principle. It links a March 2026 program review and 2025 ISMAP-LIU material. The overview does not establish that any named offering, integration or deployment qualifies.

checkedSources.title: ISMAP overview (Japanese)
checkedSources.supports: Program purpose, service-level registration, LIU scope, and procurement principle.

checkedSources.title: ISMAP Overview (English)
checkedSources.supports: English corroboration of procurement from registered service list in principle.

references.jurisdictionAndScope: Japan government information-system cloud procurement under ISMAP/ISMAP-LIU; service-list scope, not supplier-wide approval.
uncertainty: Check current exact service entry, version, scope and list status.
Check procuring body, workload, integrations, information type and procurement instructions.
ISMAP-LIU is lower-impact SaaS eligibility, not a general substitute for ISMAP.
references.proposedClaim: Japan's ISMAP program evaluates and registers cloud services on the applicable ISMAP or ISMAP-LIU list; official guidance describes list-based procurement as the general principle. Verify the exact service entry, scope, low-impact eligibility and procurement instructions. A supplier listing does not approve every offering or deployment.
references.linkedRequirement: Model exact service registration scope and distinct low-impact eligibility. Registration is not universal approval of every integration or information type.

references.historicalClaim: ISMAP registration does not remove the need for government bodies to address generative-AI-specific risks.
references.historicalSourceDate: Official ISMAP notice includes update 2026-01-09; first checked 2026-11-03.
references.currentFinding: The ISMAP notice remains available. It calls for separate handling of generative-AI risk; says a generative AI SaaS generally needs its own applicable registration, including external integrations; and says underlying registered IaaS/PaaS does not confer registration on an unregistered AI service. It describes a narrower registered AI development-platform case that still requires AI-specific measures. The Digital Agency published government generative-AI procurement/use guideline version 2.0 on 2026-06-12, after the ISMAP notice.

checkedSources.supports: AI risk treatment, SaaS registration, no automatic inheritance from IaaS/PaaS, narrower development-platform case.

checkedSources.title: Digital Agency publishes guideline version 2.0
checkedSources.supports: A newer government AI procurement/use guideline supersedes the 2025 edition; announcement checked, not all operative clauses.

references.jurisdictionAndScope: Japanese government procurement/use of generative AI and ISMAP service scopes; not a blanket rule for every Japanese organisation.
uncertainty: Check current exact service-list scope for the AI SaaS, external model or development platform.
Review the full 2026 Digital Agency guideline/checklist before a specific scenario; this check used the official announcement only.
No named model or deployment is approved.
references.proposedClaim: For Japanese government use, ISMAP registration does not remove separate handling of generative-AI risks. Determine whether the AI service is itself in scope; underlying registered IaaS/PaaS alone does not confer AI-service registration. The ISMAP notice describes a narrower registered AI development-platform case and still requires AI-specific measures. Apply current Digital Agency guidance to a specific use.
references.linkedRequirement: Require a separate fictional AI-use risk decision even when an underlying cloud service has eligible registration; processing changes can reopen review.

references.historicalClaim: The EDPB guide distinguishes adequacy, safeguards and derogations for transfers outside the EEA; parties and protection mechanisms matter beyond storage location.
references.historicalSourceDate: EDPB guide retrieved 2026-11-03; page shows no publication/last-review date.
references.currentFinding: The EDPB page remains available and sets three cumulative transfer indicators: a GDPR-subject controller/processor, personal data made available to another organisation, and a recipient outside the EEA or an international organisation. Chapter V conditions apply in addition to ordinary GDPR duties. The Commission overview frames rules across the EEA and lists adequacy, safeguards and derogations among other tools. GDPR Articles 44-49 provide the legal framework.

checkedSources.title: International data transfers
checkedSources.supports: Three-part EDPB transfer test and transfer mechanisms.

checkedSources.title: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, English (GDPR)
checkedSources.date: Regulation adopted 2016-04-27; Article 44-49 text indexed by EUR-Lex and checked 2026-11-04
checkedSources.supports: Legal Chapter V framework. Direct HTML open presented automated verification; official EUR-Lex indexed legal text was accessible.

references.jurisdictionAndScope: GDPR personal-data transfers across the EEA to third countries or international organisations; not universal residency, member-state procurement or defense accreditation.
uncertainty: Determine GDPR applicability and exact parties, disclosure, recipient and onward flows.
Check current mechanism and safeguards for the specific transfer; adequacy can be limited and may change.
The EDPB SME page is explanatory; the regulation and current Commission decisions govern a concrete case.
references.proposedClaim: Where GDPR applies, determine whether a subject controller or processor makes personal data available to another organisation outside the EEA or to an international organisation. If so, apply Chapter V as well as ordinary GDPR duties, using the applicable adequacy decision, safeguard or limited derogation. Residency alone does not resolve parties, access, recipient or onward transfer.
references.linkedRequirement: Represent information flows, parties and transfer mechanisms independently of residency; do not grant member-state procurement or defence approval from an EU-wide profile.

limitations: All five original references were accessible on 2026-11-04; per-source checked URLs and page dates are recorded above.
These recommendations are not owner acceptance, gameplay activation, a legal opinion, or certification.

The 2026-11-03 review and original source pack remain preserved unchanged.
